Problem, users and objectives
80–89 %average humidity in Orellana all year: with heat, rooms stay closed
> 1,000 ppmCO2 in a full, closed room (outdoor air ≈ 420 ppm)
≈ $250a commercial CO2 monitor (NDIR sensor)
76.2 %income poverty in Orellana (2024), the highest in Ecuador

Who is it for? · closed spaces

Classrooms · students and teachers of ESPOCH Orellana
Offices and small shops with air conditioning
Test bench: a model classroom (40 × 30 × 25 cm), a closed space we can control
General objective: develop a low-cost system, based on an ESP32 and sensors, that measures estimated CO2, temperature, humidity and noise in a closed space, warns, turns on an exhaust fan by itself, and saves the data for mathematical modeling.

Differential Equations · variables and models

1 · Variables of our system

TypeVariableSource
Independentt · time (min)date/time from Java
DependentC(t) · CO2 (ppm)MQ-135
DependentT(t) · temperature (°C)DHT22
ParameterV · volume (m³)measured

ParameterG · CO2 from peoplen × CO2 per person

Humidity goes to Multivariable Calculus; noise to Communication Systems.

2 · Mixing model (CO2): what comes in − what goes out

1Model
V dCdt = G + QCext − QC
2Linear form
dCdt + kC = GV + kCext    P(t) = k ,  Q(t) = GV + kCext
3Integrating factor
u(t) = e∫k dt = ekt
4Result
C(t) = Css + (C0 − Css) e−kt
Where
k = QV how fast CO2 changes
Css = Cext + GQ where CO2 settles
Q(t) is the right side of the linear form, not the airflow Q
Methods used
✓ Linear equation + integrating factor
✓ Change of variable for ∫ektdt
u = kt   du = k dt  →  ektk
✓ Separable variables (Newton)
Newton's law (temperature)
dTdt = −k(T − Ta)  →  T(t) = Ta + (T0 − Ta) e−kt
Full procedure (11 steps) in the written report

3 · Interpretation

  • Example: room of 144 m³ with 30 people. Almost closed: over 1,000 ppm in 10 min.
  • With 7 L/s per person: over 1,000 at 19 min, stays near 1,134 ppm.
  • To stay ≤ 1,000 ppm it needs 8.6 L/s per person: that is why the device turns on the fan.
General models: V, Q and n change for each closed space. Values here are assumed; next cycle we fit k and Q with real data from the model classroom.
5
Multivariable Calculus · discomfort index

1 · A function of two variables

The DHT22 measures temperature T and humidity H at the same time. In Orellana, how hot it feels depends on both.

DI(T, H) = T − 0.55(1 − 0.01H)(T − 14.5)
Domain
D = { (T, H) : 14.5 ≤ T ≤ 45 , 0 ≤ H ≤ 100 }
Expanded
DI = 0.45T + 7.975 + 0.0055HT − 0.07975H
DI (°C)Feeling
24 – 27more than half feel discomfort
27 – 29most people feel discomfort
29 – 32everyone feels heat stress

2 · Partial derivatives

DI'(T): H stays constant
DI'(T) = 0.45 + 0.0055H
DI'(H): T stays constant
DI'(H) = 0.0055T − 0.07975 = 0.0055(T − 14.5)
Second order and mixed
DI''(T) = 0    DI''(H) = 0    DI'TH = DI'HT = 0.0055
At 30 °C and 80 %
DI'(T) = 0.45 + 0.0055(80) = 0.89
DI'(H) = 0.0055(30 − 14.5) = 0.085
DI(30, 80) = 30 − 0.55(0.2)(15.5) = 28.3
∇DI(30, 80) = (0.89 , 0.085)

3 · Interpretation

  • 28.3: most people feel discomfort.
  • +1 °C → +0.89 · +10 % humidity → +0.85: humidity weighs almost like temperature.
  • Mixed 0.0055 > 0: the more humid, the more the heat bothers.
